text.p: South Africa are eager to play Saturday's first test against France when they hope to snuff out French designs of revenge after their close defeat in the waterlogged 1995 World Cup semifinal in Durban.

"This victory has an enormous psychological significance," assistant coach Nick Mallet said after Tuesday night's 36-20 win by the Springboks reserve side over a French regional XV had put South Africa back on a winning tack.
"There is a real osmosis between the team that played today (Tuesday) and that which will play in the test. Tonight's demonstration is a message transmitted by one to the other."
South Africa badly needed to win on Tuesday after their first tour defeat, a 30-22 reverse against the French Barbarians in Brive on Saturday.
"We had arrived from Argentina where we had played superb rugby (winning all four matches) and we were perhaps too confident," said Mallet, who spent 10 years playing in France.
"In Brive we made far too many errors and that's why we lost. A second defeat would have been catastrophic.
"Given the conditions, with a slippery ball, I think we played really well. The forwards were decisive, it's true, but we also scored five lovely tries and our defence was remarkable."

The world champions will not be disappointed if the weather conditions in Bordeaux on Saturday resemble Tuesday night's which were reminiscent of the Durban match last year when the Springbok pack had the better of a tight semifinal which South Africa won 19-15.

All the tries the South Africans have conceded in two matches in France so far have been the result of sweeping moves in the backs, evidence that the Springboks are vulnerable when the ball is played out.
But the regional XV's captain, scrum-half Aubin Hueber who lost his place in the French World Cup side to Fabien Galthie for the Durban semifinal, said: "With the Boks you always know what to expect.
"They're not going to reinvent rugby, that's for sure. But what they do, they do well. They pose a formidable physical challenge and never let go. It will be hard for France."
The Springboks could draw further inspiration from the possible presence at the Bordeaux test of President Nelson Mandela, who was there when they won the World Cup.
